cityEvents.title: Horace meets the bore on the Sacra Via
cityEvents.summary: 'I was strolling by chance along the Sacra Via, as I do', when a man known only by name seized his hand. Horace could not shake him off past the Temple of Vesta, where the bore was due in court, until his opponent appeared and dragged him off: 'So Apollo saved me.'
cityEvents.locName: the Sacra Via by the Temple of Vesta

cityEvents.title: Horace's evening stroll: fortune-tellers and Marsyas
cityEvents.summary: Horace describes his carefree life: wandering around the swindling Circus and the evening Forum, stopping by the fortune-tellers, then home to a supper of leeks and chickpeas, and in the morning not having to face the statue of Marsyas, who cannot bear the face of the moneylender Novius.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus and the evening Forum by the statue of Marsyas

cityEvents.title: Witches in the gardens of Maecenas
cityEvents.summary: A wooden Priapus in Maecenas' new gardens on the Esquiline, laid over the old paupers' cemetery, tells how he scared off the witches Canidia and Sagana, digging up bones by night, with a loud crack of his fig-wood buttocks.
cityEvents.locName: the Horti Maecenatis over the old Esquiline cemetery

cityEvents.title: Agrippa sails through the Cloaca Maxima
cityEvents.summary: As aedile Agrippa repaired the water system, built 700 basins and 500 fountains, and had himself rowed through the cleaned sewers to the Tiber as a public demonstration.
cityEvents.locName: the Cloaca Maxima, outlet by the Pons Aemilius

cityEvents.title: Octavian hurls the spear of war at the Temple of Bellona
cityEvents.summary: Declaring war on Cleopatra rather than Antony, Octavian as fetial priest cast a bloodied spear from the column of war in front of the Temple of Bellona into a patch of ground treated as enemy territory.
cityEvents.locName: the Columna Bellica before the Temple of Bellona

cityEvents.title: Octavian reads Antony's will to the senate
cityEvents.summary: Octavian seized Antony's will from the Vestals and read out to the senate its provisions: legacies to Cleopatra's children and burial beside her in Alexandria. Outrage swung opinion behind war.
cityEvents.locName: taken from the Vestals' keeping; read in the senate

cityEvents.title: Business at the Puteal Libonis
cityEvents.summary: Errands pursue Horace through Rome: 'Roscius begs you to be at the Puteal tomorrow before eight', the moneylenders' meeting place by the Temple of Castor and the Arch of Augustus in the Forum.
cityEvents.locName: the Puteal Libonis, SE end of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Janus closed after Actium
cityEvents.summary: The senate decreed that the doors of the Ianus Geminus be closed, for only the third time in Roman history, to mark the end of the civil wars.
cityEvents.locName: Ianus Geminus by the Argiletum

cityEvents.title: Octavian's triple triumph
cityEvents.summary: For three days Octavian triumphed over Illyricum, Actium and Egypt; on the third an effigy of Cleopatra with the asp was carried, with her children Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene walking behind.
cityEvents.locName: triumphal route along the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Temple of Divus Iulius dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Octavian dedicated the temple of his deified father on the cremation site, its platform decorated with the beaks of ships from Actium, and held lavish games.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Divus Iulius, E end of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Curia Iulia dedicated with the statue and altar of Victory
cityEvents.summary: Octavian dedicated Caesar's new senate house and set inside it the statue of Victory from Tarentum on a globe, with an altar where senators offered incense before sessions; the altar would be fought over four centuries later.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Iulia, NW side of the Forum

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Temple of Apollo on the Palatine dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Octavian dedicated the gleaming Luna-marble temple of Apollo next to his house, with the portico of the Danaids and the Greek and Latin libraries; Propertius describes the doors of ivory and the chariot of the Sun on the roof.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Apollo Palatinus

cityEvents.title: Laurels and the civic crown at Augustus' door
cityEvents.summary: The senate named Octavian Augustus and decreed that the doorposts of his Palatine house be wreathed with laurel and an oak wreath, the civic crown for saving citizens, be fixed above the door.
cityEvents.locName: the entrance of Augustus' house on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Marcellus the first to be laid in the Mausoleum
cityEvents.summary: Augustus' nephew and heir Marcellus died at 19 and was the first buried in the new Mausoleum in the Campus Martius; Virgil's lament in Aeneid 6 made Octavia faint when he read it to her.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Augustus

cityEvents.title: Flood carries off the Pons Sublicius
cityEvents.summary: In the year of Augustus' illness the Tiber rose, swept away the wooden bridge and made the city navigable by boat for three days.
cityEvents.locName: the Pons Sublicius

cityEvents.title: Famine crowd besieges the senate to make Augustus dictator
cityEvents.summary: During plague and famine the people shut the senators in the Curia and threatened to burn them alive unless they voted Augustus the dictatorship; Augustus refused on his knees, baring his breast, and took the grain supply instead.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Iulia

cityEvents.title: The Golden Milestone set up
cityEvents.summary: As curator of the roads, Augustus set up a gilded bronze column at the head of the Forum near the Temple of Saturn, listing the distances to the main cities of the empire.
cityEvents.locName: Miliarium Aureum at the S end of the Rostra by the Temple of Saturn

cityEvents.title: Horace's book longs for the Sosii brothers' shop
cityEvents.summary: Horace teases his first book of Epistles, polished with the pumice of the Sosii, the booksellers, for eyeing 'Vertumnus and Janus' where it hopes to be put on sale, and predicts it will end up in the provinces as a schoolbook.
cityEvents.locName: the Sosii brothers' shop by the statue of Vertumnus and the arches of Janus

cityEvents.title: Altar of Fortuna Redux at the Porta Capena
cityEvents.summary: For Augustus' return from the East the senate consecrated an altar of Fortune the Home-bringer by the Porta Capena, beside the temples of Honos and Virtus; the day became the Augustalia.
cityEvents.locName: beside the Porta Capena, by the Temple of Honos and Virtus

cityEvents.title: Night sacrifices at the Tarentum: Secular Games
cityEvents.summary: On the night of 31 May Augustus sacrificed nine ewes and nine she-goats to the Moirai on three altars by the Tiber at the Tarentum, with stage plays on a lit stage without seats; Agrippa joined him on the following nights.
cityEvents.locName: the Tarentum by the Tiber in the NW Campus Martius
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
cityEvents.note: The inscribed Acta were found in 1890 near the Tiber by Corso Vittorio Emanuele, close to the Tarentum.

cityEvents.title: Horace's Carmen Saeculare sung on the Palatine and Capitol
cityEvents.summary: On the last day 27 boys and 27 girls sang Horace's hymn before the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine and again on the Capitol. 'Carmen composuit Q. Horatius Flaccus', records the inscription.
cityEvents.locName: before the Temple of Apollo Palatinus, then on the Capitol

cityEvents.title: The statue of Vertumnus speaks in the Vicus Tuscus
cityEvents.summary: In Propertius' elegy the bronze statue of the Etruscan god Vertumnus, standing at the Forum end of the Vicus Tuscus, tells passers-by how he can be any shape and how he once was carved of maple.
cityEvents.locName: the signum Vortumni at the Forum end of the Vicus Tuscus

cityEvents.title: Theatre of Marcellus dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Augustus dedicated the theatre named for his nephew; during the games a tame tiger was shown for the first time and Augustus' curule chair collapsed beneath him.
cityEvents.locName: Theatre of Marcellus

cityEvents.title: The street that sells incense, perfume and pepper
cityEvents.summary: Horace imagines his bad poems used as wrapping paper in 'the street that sells incense, perfumes and pepper', the Vicus Tuscus.
cityEvents.locName: the Vicus Tuscus

cityEvents.title: Agrippa laid in the Mausoleum of Augustus
cityEvents.summary: Augustus delivered the funeral oration over his friend and son-in-law with a curtain hung between himself and the body, then placed his remains in his own Mausoleum.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Augustus

cityEvents.title: Augustus becomes pontifex maximus and brings Vesta to the Palatine
cityEvents.summary: Elected chief priest by a crowd from all Italy, Augustus did not move into the Domus Publica but gave it to the Vestals, made part of his own house public property and set up a shrine of Vesta beside it.
cityEvents.locName: Augustus' Palatine house, with the new shrine of Vesta

cityEvents.title: Obelisk of Rameses II raised on the spina of the Circus
cityEvents.summary: Augustus brought an obelisk from Heliopolis and set it up on the dividing barrier of the Circus Maximus, dedicated to the Sun, to mark the conquest of Egypt.
cityEvents.locName: the spina of the Circus Maximus
cityEvents.note: Now in Piazza del Popolo (Flaminio obelisk).

cityEvents.title: The obelisk sundial of the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: A second Egyptian obelisk became the gnomon of a huge meridian laid out in bronze letters on the pavement of the northern Campus Martius, near the Ara Pacis.
cityEvents.locName: the meridian of Augustus, N Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Drusus' funeral: laudations in the Forum and Circus Flaminius
cityEvents.summary: The body of Drusus, dead in Germany, was escorted to Rome by Tiberius on foot. Tiberius spoke the laudation in the Forum and Augustus, who could not enter the city in mourning while holding command, spoke in the Circus Flaminius; the ashes went into the Mausoleum.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Flaminius, outside the pomerium

cityEvents.title: Ara Pacis Augustae dedicated
cityEvents.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, voted on his return from Spain and Gaul in 13 BC, was dedicated beside the Via Flaminia on Livia's birthday.
cityEvents.locName: original site of the Ara Pacis by the Via Flaminia (under Palazzo Fiano)

cityEvents.title: Porticus of Livia built on the site of Vedius Pollio's house
cityEvents.summary: Augustus razed the extravagant house on the Oppian left to him by Vedius Pollio, who fed slaves to his lampreys, and built there a public portico in Livia's name with a shrine of Concord.
cityEvents.locName: Porticus Liviae on the Oppian (Esquiline) near the Clivus Suburanus

cityEvents.title: Rome divided into 14 regions and 265 vici; compital shrines rebuilt
cityEvents.summary: After a fire around the Forum, Augustus reorganised the city into regions and neighbourhoods, each with elected vicomagistri who tended the Lares Augusti at the crossroads shrines. The altar of the Vicus Sandalarius (2 BC) shows Augustus with Livia and Gaius.
cityEvents.locName: compitum of the Vicus Sandalarius near the Templum Pacis (example)

cityEvents.title: Compitalia at the crossroads shrines
cityEvents.summary: At the winter Compitalia every neighbourhood decorated its crossroads shrine, hung woollen dolls and balls for each free person and slave, and the vicomagistri in purple-bordered togas offered to the Lares; Augustus' reform tied the cult to his genius.
cityEvents.locName: a compitum in the Subura
cityEvents.note: Annual; marker at a representative Subura crossroads.

cityEvents.title: Battle of Salamis restaged in Augustus' naval basin
cityEvents.summary: Augustus dug a basin 1800 by 1200 Roman feet across the Tiber for a mock sea battle of Athenians and Persians with 30 warships and 3000 fighters; Ovid recommends the crowds as good hunting for lovers.
cityEvents.locName: Naumachia Augusti in Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Julia's night revels at the Rostra and the statue of Marsyas
cityEvents.summary: Augustus learned that his daughter Julia had held drunken revels in the Forum by night, on the very Rostra from which he had proposed his laws on adultery, and had crowned the statue of Marsyas. He exiled her to Pandateria.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra and the statue of Marsyas in the Forum
cityEvents.note: The Marsyas statue stood by the tribunal of the praetor near the Comitium; marker placed between the Rostra and the Lacus Curtius.

cityEvents.title: Ovid: take a stroll in Pompey's portico
cityEvents.summary: The Ars Amatoria sends the would-be lover to saunter in the shade of Pompey's portico in summer, then to the porticoes of Octavia and Livia and the colonnade of the Danaids.
cityEvents.locName: the Porticus of Pompey behind the theatre

cityEvents.title: Ovid: lawyers fall in love at the Appiades fountain
cityEvents.summary: Even the courts are good hunting: at the fountain of the Appiades by the Temple of Venus in Caesar's forum, Ovid jokes, the advocate is caught by love and can no longer argue his own case.
cityEvents.locName: the Appiades fountain before the Temple of Venus Genetrix

cityEvents.title: Ovid: sit close in the Circus
cityEvents.summary: In the Circus Maximus, says Ovid, no one stops you sitting thigh to thigh with a girl; ask whose horses are coming, brush dust from her dress, and back her favourite.
cityEvents.locName: the seating of the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Ovid: the temple of the Memphian heifer
cityEvents.summary: Ovid warns that the temple of Isis in the Campus Martius makes many girls what Io was to Jupiter, a place of assignations.
cityEvents.locName: the Iseum Campense

cityEvents.title: Augustus hailed Father of his Country
cityEvents.summary: After the plebs had acclaimed him at the theatre, Messalla spoke for the senate in the Curia, naming Augustus Pater Patriae; with tears in his eyes he replied that he had attained his highest hopes.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Iulia

cityEvents.title: Forum of Augustus and Temple of Mars Ultor dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Forty years after the vow at Philippi, Augustus dedicated the temple of Mars the Avenger in his new forum, with the recovered Parthian standards inside and statues of the great men of Rome in the porticoes.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus

cityEvents.title: Ovid's last night in Rome, gazing at the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: Ordered into exile, Ovid spent his last night in his house beside the Capitol, looking up at the temples 'joined in vain to my household' and praying to their gods before leaving at dawn.
cityEvents.locName: Ovid's house near the Capitol
cityEvents.note: Ovid says his house adjoined the Capitol; exact site unknown.

cityEvents.title: The Lupercalia: the run around the Palatine
cityEvents.summary: Goats and a dog were sacrificed in the Lupercal cave; youths smeared with blood and laughing, naked but for goatskins, ran around the Palatine striking women with thongs of hide to make them fertile.
cityEvents.locName: from the Lupercal around the foot of the Palatine
cityEvents.note: Annual rite on 15 February, celebrated until the 490s.

cityEvents.title: Megalesia: the Galli process for the Great Mother
cityEvents.summary: At the April games of Cybele the eunuch Galli paraded the goddess with drums, cymbals and pipes, and plays were staged before her temple on the Palatine.
cityEvents.locName: before the Temple of Magna Mater on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Parilia: leaping the bonfires on Rome's birthday
cityEvents.summary: On the birthday of the city shepherds and citizens purified themselves with ash and bean stalks from the Vestals and leapt over bonfires of straw; Ovid says he did so himself.
cityEvents.locName: the Palatine, by the hut of Romulus

cityEvents.title: The Argei: straw men thrown from the Sublician bridge
cityEvents.summary: On the Ides of May the Vestals threw 27 rush puppets in human shape from the wooden Pons Sublicius into the Tiber, a rite whose meaning puzzled Ovid and his contemporaries.
cityEvents.locName: the Pons Sublicius
cityEvents.note: Annual rite; Ovid's account dated to the Fasti (c. AD 8).

cityEvents.title: A barefoot matron on the Nova Via at the Vestalia
cityEvents.summary: Returning from the Vestalia, Ovid met a barefoot matron coming down the Nova Via where it joins the Forum; an old woman explained that the place was once a marsh, before the Velabrum was drained.
cityEvents.locName: the Nova Via where it joins the Forum

cityEvents.title: 'Quinctilius Varus, give me back my legions!'
cityEvents.summary: At the news of the loss of three legions in Germany, Augustus did not shave for months and at times beat his head against the doors of his house crying out to Varus to return the legions.
cityEvents.locName: Augustus' house on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Ovid's exiled book walks the Sacra Via
cityEvents.summary: In Tristia 3.1 Ovid's book arrives in Rome and is led from the Forum of Caesar along the Sacra Via, past the Temple of Vesta and the Regia, to the old Porta Palatii and the Temple of Jupiter Stator.
cityEvents.locName: the Sacra Via past the Temple of Vesta and the Regia

cityEvents.title: Ovid's book at Augustus' door
cityEvents.summary: The book stares at the doorposts of Augustus' house, decked with arms and laurel and the oak crown, and wonders whether this is the house of Jupiter.
cityEvents.locName: doorway of Augustus' house on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Ovid's book turned away by Rome's libraries
cityEvents.summary: The book climbs to the Palatine library by the Temple of Apollo and is refused, then tries the library in the Porticus Octaviae and the Atrium Libertatis, the first public library, and is refused again.
cityEvents.locName: the Palatine library at the Temple of Apollo; also the Porticus Octaviae and Atrium Libertatis

cityEvents.title: Tiberius rededicates the Temple of Concord
cityEvents.summary: Tiberius rebuilt the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol from his German spoils, filling it with Greek masterpieces, and dedicated it in his own and his dead brother Drusus' names.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Concord

cityEvents.title: Circus flooded; races held in the Forum of Augustus
cityEvents.summary: The Tiber flooded the Circus Maximus so badly that the horse races of the Ludi Martiales were held in the Forum of Augustus instead.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum of Augustus, used as a racetrack

cityEvents.title: Augustus' funeral orations in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Augustus' wax image lay on a gold and ivory couch; Drusus read a eulogy from the old Rostra and Tiberius the main laudation from the Rostra of the Temple of Divus Iulius.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra of the Temple of Divus Iulius and the Rostra Vetera

cityEvents.title: Augustus cremated in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: Senators carried the body through the Porta Triumphalis to the pyre in the Campus Martius; an eagle was released from the flames and the ex-praetor Numerius Atticus swore he saw Augustus ascend. Livia gathered the bones for five days and laid them in the Mausoleum.
cityEvents.locName: the ustrinum of Augustus near the Mausoleum, N Campus Martius
cityEvents.note: Strabo describes the ustrinum of white marble with an iron railing near the Mausoleum.

cityEvents.title: Tiber floods the low city; curators of the river appointed
cityEvents.summary: Continuous rain raised the Tiber over the low parts of the city, wrecking houses and drowning people; the senate debated diverting its tributaries, and Tiberius created a board to manage the river.
cityEvents.locName: low-lying districts along the river

cityEvents.title: Germanicus' triumph; arch by the Temple of Saturn
cityEvents.summary: Germanicus triumphed over the Germans with the recovered standards of Varus; an arch near the Temple of Saturn commemorated their recovery.
cityEvents.locName: the Arch of Tiberius beside the Temple of Saturn

cityEvents.title: The scandal of Paulina in the temple of Isis
cityEvents.summary: The knight Mundus bribed priests of Isis to tell the noble matron Paulina that the god Anubis desired her; she spent the night in the temple with Mundus. Tiberius crucified the priests, razed the temple and threw the statue of Isis into the Tiber.
cityEvents.locName: the temple of Isis in the Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Germanicus' ashes laid in the Mausoleum
cityEvents.summary: Agrippina carried the urn from Brundisium; on the day it was placed in the Mausoleum the Campus Martius blazed with torches and crowds cried that the state had fallen.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Augustus and the Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Crowd drags Piso's statues to the Gemonian Stairs
cityEvents.summary: During the trial of Cn. Piso for the death of Germanicus, the crowd outside the Curia dragged his statues to the Gemonian Stairs and was about to smash them. Piso's house, decorated for a banquet, looked down on the Forum.
cityEvents.locName: the Scalae Gemoniae below the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Theatre of Pompey burns; Tiberius rebuilds it
cityEvents.summary: The scaena of Pompey's theatre burned; Tiberius promised to rebuild it under Pompey's name, and a statue of Sejanus was set up there for his part in saving the rest of the building.
cityEvents.locName: the stage building of the Theatre of Pompey

cityEvents.title: Sejanus concentrates the guard in the Castra Praetoria
cityEvents.summary: Sejanus gathered the nine praetorian cohorts, until then billeted around the city and Italy, into one fortified camp on the NE edge of Rome, a base that would make and unmake emperors.
cityEvents.locName: the Castra Praetoria beyond the Viminal

cityEvents.title: Fire on the Caelian; a statue of Tiberius survives
cityEvents.summary: A fire devastated the Caelian. Only a statue of Tiberius in the house of the senator Junius was untouched, and the senate proposed renaming the hill Mons Augustus.
cityEvents.locName: the Caelian hill

cityEvents.title: Crowd surrounds the Curia with images of Agrippina
cityEvents.summary: When Tiberius' letter against Agrippina and her son Nero was read, the people gathered around the senate house carrying their portraits and shouting that the letter was forged.
cityEvents.locName: around the Curia Iulia

cityEvents.title: Tiberius' 'verbose and grand letter' read to the senate
cityEvents.summary: Sejanus came to the senate meeting in the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine expecting the tribunician power. The long letter from Capri ended by ordering his arrest; Macro had already replaced his guards with the vigiles.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Apollo Palatinus

cityEvents.title: Sejanus condemned in the Temple of Concord
cityEvents.summary: Led to the prison, Sejanus was condemned to death the same day by the senate meeting in the Temple of Concord next to the Carcer, while the crowd smashed his statues.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Concord next to the Carcer

cityEvents.title: Sejanus' body on the Gemonian Stairs
cityEvents.summary: Sejanus was strangled in the Carcer and his body thrown down the Gemonian Stairs, where the mob abused it for three days before it was dragged with a hook into the Tiber; his children were later killed too.
cityEvents.locName: the Scalae Gemoniae from the Carcer toward the Capitol
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityEvents.title: Credit crash in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Enforcement of the old usury laws forced creditors to call in loans; land prices collapsed and debtors were ruined until Tiberius put up 100 million sesterces of interest-free loans through banks.
cityEvents.locName: the bankers around the Ianus Medius and the Basilica Aemilia

cityEvents.title: Drusus Caesar starved in a palace cellar
cityEvents.summary: Germanicus' son Drusus, held in an underground room of the Palatine, died of hunger after chewing the stuffing of his mattress; Tiberius had the record of his last words read to the senate.
cityEvents.locName: a basement room of the Palatine palace

cityEvents.title: Fire on the Aventine and the Circus
cityEvents.summary: A fire burned the part of the Circus Maximus next to the Aventine and the Aventine itself; Tiberius paid out 100 million sesterces in compensation.
cityEvents.locName: the Aventine and the adjacent side of the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: 'Tiberius to the Tiber!'
cityEvents.summary: At the news of Tiberius' death the crowd shouted that his body should be thrown in the Tiber. It was brought to Rome, cremated in the Campus Martius with a eulogy by Caligula, and laid in the Mausoleum.
cityEvents.locName: the Campus Martius and the Mausoleum of Augustus

cityEvents.title: Caligula's bridge over the Temple of Augustus
cityEvents.summary: Caligula extended the palace down to the Forum, making the Temple of Castor its vestibule, where he would sit between the twin gods to be worshipped, and built a bridge over the Temple of Divus Augustus to link the Palatine with the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Castor used as palace vestibule; bridge to the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Caligula scatters money from the roof of the Basilica Julia
cityEvents.summary: For several days Caligula threw large sums of coins down to the crowd from the roof of the Basilica Julia.
cityEvents.locName: the roof of the Basilica Julia

cityEvents.title: Caligula's body half-burned in the Lamian Gardens
cityEvents.summary: Caligula's corpse was carried secretly to the Horti Lamiani on the Esquiline, half-burned and lightly buried; his ghost was said to haunt the place until his sisters reburied him.
cityEvents.locName: the Horti Lamiani on the Esquiline

cityEvents.title: Caligula murdered in a palace passage
cityEvents.summary: Leaving the Palatine games at midday, Caligula took a covered passage (crypta) toward the palace to see some boys from Asia rehearsing; the tribunes Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus struck him down with thirty wounds.
cityEvents.locName: a covered passage (crypta) of the Palatine palace near the temporary theatre
cityEvents.note: Often linked to the surviving cryptoporticus under the Domus Tiberiana, which is in part later (Neronian).

cityEvents.title: Claudius found behind a curtain and carried to the camp
cityEvents.summary: Terrified, Claudius hid behind a curtain in a room of the palace called the Hermaeum; a soldier saw his feet, hailed him emperor and he was carried in a litter to the Castra Praetoria, where he promised each soldier 15,000 sesterces.
cityEvents.locName: from the Hermaeum in the palace to the Castra Praetoria

cityEvents.title: Claudius climbs the Capitol steps on his knees
cityEvents.summary: Celebrating his British triumph, Claudius climbed the steps to the Capitoline temple on his knees, supported by his sons-in-law.
cityEvents.locName: the steps up to the Capitoline temple

cityEvents.title: Claudius frees sick slaves left on the Tiber Island
cityEvents.summary: Owners abandoned sick and worn-out slaves on the island of Aesculapius to avoid the cost of care; Claudius decreed that any such slave who recovered was free.
cityEvents.locName: the sanctuary of Aesculapius on the Tiber Island

cityEvents.title: Messalina killed in the Gardens of Lucullus
cityEvents.summary: After her bigamous marriage to C. Silius, Messalina fled to the Horti Lucullani on the Pincian, the gardens she had coveted from Valerius Asiaticus; a tribune sent by Narcissus ran her through as her mother Lepida urged her to die with dignity.
cityEvents.locName: the Horti Lucullani on the Pincian

cityEvents.title: Claudius expels the Jews 'stirred up by Chrestus'
cityEvents.summary: Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were constantly rioting at the instigation of 'Chrestus', probably disputes over Jesus in the synagogues; Aquila and Priscilla left for Corinth. The Jewish community lived mainly across the Tiber.
cityEvents.locName: the Jewish quarter of Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Claudius pelted with bread crusts in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: With only fifteen days' grain left, a mob caught Claudius in the middle of the Forum and pelted him with abuse and crusts, until he escaped through a back door into the palace.
cityEvents.locName: the middle of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Caratacus before Claudius at the Praetorian Camp
cityEvents.summary: The captured British king was paraded with his family before the praetorians drawn up on the field in front of their camp; his speech to Claudius won pardon for him and his family.
cityEvents.locName: the parade ground before the Castra Praetoria

cityEvents.title: Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus reach the city
cityEvents.summary: Claudius opened the two highest aqueducts of Rome on 1 August; their arcades crossed the Via Praenestina and Labicana in a monumental double gate, later part of the Aurelian Wall as Porta Maggiore.
cityEvents.locName: the double arch of the aqueducts (Porta Maggiore)

cityEvents.title: Nero presented at the Praetorian Camp
cityEvents.summary: At noon on the day Claudius' death was announced, the doors of the palace opened and Nero went out with the prefect Burrus to the cohort on guard, was put in a litter and taken to the camp to be hailed emperor.
cityEvents.locName: from the palace steps to the Castra Praetoria

cityEvents.title: Slave dealers at the Temple of Castor
cityEvents.summary: Seneca, discussing insults, describes the slave dealers whose 'cages' of wretched slaves stood by the Temple of Castor; Plautus already placed shady dealers behind it.
cityEvents.locName: beside the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Britannicus poisoned at the imperial table
cityEvents.summary: At dinner in the palace a cold-water chaser carried poison to Britannicus, who collapsed; Nero said it was epilepsy. He was buried in the Campus Martius that same night in a torrential downpour.
cityEvents.locName: the dining room of the palace on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Nero's wooden amphitheatre in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: Nero built a huge timber amphitheatre in the Campus Martius in a year, where he gave shows in which no one, not even a criminal, was killed.
cityEvents.locName: Nero's amphitheatre in the Campus Martius (site unknown)

cityEvents.title: Nero's Juvenalia in the Grove of the Caesars
cityEvents.summary: To celebrate his first shave Nero held private games, the Juvenalia, in the grove by Augustus' naval basin across the Tiber, with booths selling luxuries; senators and old matrons were made to perform, and Nero sang to the lyre.
cityEvents.locName: the Nemus Caesarum by the Naumachia Augusti, Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Crowd restores Octavia's statues and smashes Poppaea's
cityEvents.summary: At a rumour that Nero had recalled his divorced wife Octavia, the people climbed the Capitol, threw down the statues of Poppaea and carried Octavia's garlanded statues into the Forum and the temples.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol and the Forum

cityEvents.title: Tigellinus' banquet on the Pool of Agrippa
cityEvents.summary: Tigellinus gave Nero a feast on a raft towed by gilded boats on the Stagnum Agrippae, with brothels on the banks; days later Nero went through a mock wedding with the freedman Pythagoras.
cityEvents.locName: the Stagnum Agrippae by the Baths of Agrippa

cityEvents.title: Christians burned as torches in Nero's gardens
cityEvents.summary: To divert blame Nero punished the Christians: some were dressed in animal skins and torn by dogs, others crucified or set alight as night lamps in his gardens across the Tiber, while Nero mingled with the crowd dressed as a charioteer.
cityEvents.locName: Nero's gardens and circus in the Ager Vaticanus

cityEvents.title: Peter crucified near the obelisk of the Vatican circus
cityEvents.summary: Tradition places Peter's martyrdom in Nero's circus on the Vatican, 'between the two turning posts' near the obelisk, and his burial in the cemetery on the slope beside it, where the 'trophy' was shown by c. 200.
cityEvents.locName: the spina of the Circus of Gaius and Nero by the obelisk

cityEvents.title: Nero's Golden House rises from the ruins
cityEvents.summary: On land cleared by the fire Nero built the Domus Aurea, a country estate in the city with a lake where the Colosseum now stands, a 120-foot colossus of himself in the vestibule and a revolving dining room: 'At last I can live like a human being.'
cityEvents.locName: the Esquiline (Oppian) pavilion of the Domus Aurea

cityEvents.title: Nero sings the Fall of Troy from the tower of Maecenas
cityEvents.summary: Suetonius says Nero watched the blaze from the tower in the gardens of Maecenas and, delighted by 'the beauty of the flames', sang the sack of Troy in stage costume; Tacitus reports it as a rumour that he sang on his private stage.
cityEvents.locName: the tower in the Horti Maecenatis on the Esquiline
